meta.accuracyNote: Summaries paraphrase the Quranic narratives cited for each story. No quotations, events, dates, or hadith references have been invented. 'tradition' = 'quran' means the story is told in the cited verses; 'quran+scholarship' means the Quran gives a brief account and further detail comes from classical scholarly retellings — those details are labelled as such. The daily rotation is a reading schedule only; it does NOT claim any prophet's story happened on today's calendar date. Hadith references are intentionally omitted unless verified; add them only with a checked source.
meta.title: Daily Prophets' Stories

stories.context: The Quran introduces Adam as the first human and the first prophet, taught the names of things and placed on earth as a trustee.
lessons: Knowledge and learning are a trust, not a privilege.
Arrogance — refusing to bow when commanded — is the root of Iblis's fall.
Repentance is always open to the one who turns back sincerely.
stories.summary: Allah created Adam, taught him the names of things, and commanded the angels to bow to him. Iblis refused out of pride. Adam and his wife were placed in the Garden with one command not to approach a particular tree.
stories.title: Adam — Creation and the Trust

stories.context: After eating from the forbidden tree, Adam and his wife acknowledged their wrongdoing and turned to Allah in repentance.
lessons: Admitting a mistake is the first step back, not a defeat.
Blaming others prolongs the fall; owning it ends it.
Forgiveness follows sincere repentance.
stories.summary: Deceived by Iblis, Adam and his wife ate from the tree they had been warned about. They immediately confessed their wrongdoing and asked for forgiveness, and Allah accepted their repentance and guided them.
stories.title: Adam — The Fall and Repentance

stories.context: The Quran tells of the two sons of Adam and the first murder on earth, a story about envy and the sanctity of life.
lessons: Envy, left unchecked, grows into violence.
A sincere offering is accepted for its sincerity, not its size.
Every life is sacred; taking one unjustly is a grave wrong.
stories.summary: Two sons of Adam each made an offering; one was accepted and the other was not. Consumed by envy, the rejected brother killed the accepted one, then learned — from a raven burying its dead — how to hide his brother's body, and was filled with remorse.
stories.title: The Two Sons of Adam — Envy and the First Wrongdoing
stories.titleBn: আদমের দুই পুত্র — হিংসা ও প্রথম অপরাধ

stories.context: Idris is mentioned only briefly in the Quran, honoured as a truthful prophet raised to a high station.
lessons: Truthfulness is itself a form of greatness.
A short mention in revelation is still an honour.
Steadfastness matters more than fame.
stories.summary: The Quran describes Idris as a man of truth and a prophet, raised by Allah to a high station. Classical scholars retell his story as one of wisdom, patience and devotion; the Quran itself gives no further narrative detail.
stories.title: Idris — The Truthful Prophet

stories.context: Nuh called his people for centuries to worship Allah alone. The Quran says he remained among them for 950 years.
lessons: Persistence in a good cause is measured in decades, not days.
Mockery is not evidence that a message is false.
A caller must keep advising even when results are slow.
stories.summary: Nuh warned his people night and day, in public and in private, but most of them plugged their ears and mocked him. Only a few believed. He prayed for guidance for his people until Allah commanded him to build the Ark.
stories.title: Nuh — Nine Hundred and Fifty Years of Calling

stories.context: When the flood came, the Ark carried Nuh, the believers, and pairs of living creatures. His own son chose the mountain over the Ark and was lost.
lessons: Salvation comes through obedience, not family ties.
Preparation before the crisis is what saves during it.
Even a prophet cannot save one who refuses to board.
stories.summary: Under Allah's command, Nuh built the Ark while his people laughed. When the flood came, the believers boarded with pairs of creatures. The waters covered the land, and the Ark came to rest. Nuh's son, who refused to board, was among those lost.
stories.title: Nuh — The Ark and the Flood

stories.context: Hud was sent to 'Ad, a powerful people famed for their strength and tall structures, who worshipped idols and oppressed others.
lessons: Strength without gratitude becomes arrogance.
Prosperity is a test, not proof of being right.
A people's greatness is measured by justice, not buildings.
stories.summary: Hud called the people of 'Ad to worship Allah alone and abandon their idols. They boasted of their strength and demanded a sign. A barren wind came upon them for days, and the rejecting people were destroyed while Hud and the believers were saved.
stories.title: Hud — The People of 'Ad

stories.context: Salih was sent to Thamud, who carved homes into rock. He gave them a she-camel as a sign and warned them not to harm it.
lessons: A clear sign does not help those who refuse to see.
Harming what Allah has protected invites ruin.
Wealth and skill cannot protect a people from their own injustice.
stories.summary: Salih called Thamud to Allah and gave them a she-camel as a sign, with the right to drink on appointed days. They hamstrung the camel despite the warning. After three days, a mighty blast seized them, and Salih and the believers were saved.
stories.title: Salih — The She-Camel

stories.context: Young Ibrahim reasoned with his people against idol worship, then confronted the idols themselves in the temple.
lessons: Truth can be spoken respectfully and still firmly.
An argument that exposes a contradiction is stronger than shouting.
Blind imitation of ancestors is not a proof.
stories.summary: Ibrahim asked his people why they worshipped idols that could neither hear nor help. When they were away, he broke the idols except the largest, then challenged them: if the idols could speak, let them say who did it. His people had no answer but anger.
stories.title: Ibrahim — Breaking the Idols

stories.context: For breaking the idols, Ibrahim was thrown into a fire. Allah made the fire cool and safe for him.
lessons: Courage means standing firm when the cost is real.
Allah's protection can come in the very place of danger.
A crowd's verdict is not Allah's verdict.
stories.summary: Ibrahim's people decided to burn him for breaking their idols. They lit a great fire and cast him into it. Allah commanded the fire to be cool and safe, and Ibrahim emerged unharmed, while his persecutors' plan came to nothing.
stories.title: Ibrahim — The Fire Made Cool

stories.context: Ibrahim dreamed that he was sacrificing his son. Both father and son submitted, and Allah ransomed the son with a great sacrifice.
lessons: Submission means trusting Allah even when the command is hard to bear.
A son's willingness honours a father's faith.
Relief comes at the very point of complete surrender.
stories.summary: Ibrahim told his son of the dream, and the son replied that his father should do as commanded and would find him patient. As Ibrahim prepared to act, Allah called out that the vision had been fulfilled, and ransomed the son with a mighty sacrifice.
stories.title: Ibrahim — The Sacrifice and the Son

stories.context: Ibrahim and Ismail raised the foundations of the House at Makkah and prayed that Allah accept it and make their descendants a submitting community.
lessons: Building for Allah is completed with prayer, not pride.
A house of worship begins with a family working together.
Every good work should end with asking for acceptance.
stories.summary: Ibrahim and his son Ismail raised the foundations of the House, praying that Allah accept their work, teach their descendants the rites, and send them a messenger to recite the signs and purify them.
stories.title: Ibrahim — Building the House

stories.context: Lut called his people, who had fallen into shameful practices, to fear Allah and abandon their corruption.
lessons: A prophet must speak against his own people's wrongdoing.
Hospitality and honouring guests are sacred duties.
When corruption is complete, leaving is obedience, not escape.
stories.summary: Lut warned his people against their shameful deeds, but they threatened to expel him. Angels came to him in human form; his people rushed to his house, and he pleaded with them to honour his guests. At dawn, his town was overturned, and Lut and the believers were saved.
stories.title: Lut — The Call to His People

stories.context: Ismail, left with his mother Hajar in a barren valley, became part of the story of Makkah and the well of Zamzam in classical retellings.
lessons: Provision can appear where no cause is visible.
A mother's search and a child's thirst are remembered in rites of worship.
Trust in Allah turns a barren valley into a city.
stories.summary: The Quran records Ibrahim's prayer for the valley where he settled part of his family, asking that it be safe and provided for. Classical scholars retell how Hajar searched between the hills and how the well of Zamzam sprang forth — details that come from tradition, not from these verses themselves.
stories.title: Ismail — The Valley and the Well

stories.context: Ishaq was announced to Ibrahim and Sarah in their old age, a glad tiding that seemed impossible to them.
lessons: Allah's promise is not bound by human calculations of age.
Good news may arrive when hope seems finished.
Gratitude for a child is part of the blessing itself.
stories.summary: Angels visiting Ibrahim brought glad tidings of a knowledgeable son. Sarah laughed in wonder, for she was old and her husband aged. The angels replied that this was Allah's decree, and Ishaq was born, a prophet among the righteous.
stories.title: Ishaq — The Glad Tidings

stories.context: Yaqub, father of Yusuf, endured the loss of his beloved son and later his sight, yet never stopped trusting Allah.
lessons: Grief and faith can live in the same heart.
A parent's patience can span decades without bitterness.
Hope in Allah does not expire with time.
stories.summary: When Yusuf was lost, Yaqub wept until he lost his sight, yet he told his sons never to despair of Allah's relief. Years later, when the truth came out, he forgave his sons and prayed for them, and his family was reunited in Egypt.
stories.title: Yaqub — Patience and Trust

stories.context: As a boy, Yusuf dreamed that eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowed to him. His father warned him not to tell his brothers.
lessons: A great dream should be guarded, not advertised.
Envy often begins among those closest to us.
A father's warning is itself a form of protection.
stories.summary: Yusuf told his father Yaqub that he had seen eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowing down to him. Yaqub understood the dream's meaning, warned him not to recount it to his brothers lest envy stir them, and told him Allah would complete His favour upon him.
stories.title: Yusuf — The Dream

stories.context: Yusuf's brothers, jealous of their father's love, threw him into a well and told their father a wolf had eaten him.
lessons: Jealousy can make brothers into strangers.
A lie needs a prop; truth needs only patience.
Even in a well, a boy can be under Allah's care.
stories.summary: The brothers lured Yusuf away, cast him into a well, and stained his shirt with false blood. A caravan passing by drew him out and sold him in Egypt for a small price. In the house of his Egyptian master, Yusuf grew in wisdom and beauty.
stories.title: Yusuf — The Well and the Caravan

stories.context: In Egypt, Yusuf resisted temptation in his master's house and was imprisoned on a false charge, where he remained for years.
lessons: Chastity is strength, not weakness.
A false charge can still lead to honour in the end.
Prison can become a school for a patient heart.
stories.summary: The wife of Yusuf's master tried to seduce him; he refused and fled, and the torn shirt proved his innocence — yet he was imprisoned to protect reputations. In prison he called his fellow inmates to Allah and interpreted their dreams with a clarity that amazed them.
stories.title: Yusuf — Trials in Egypt

stories.context: The king dreamed of seven fat cows eaten by seven lean ones, and seven green ears of grain and seven dry. Yusuf interpreted the dream and planned for the famine.
lessons: Knowledge is most valuable when it serves people in need.
Planning for hardship is part of trust, not a lack of it.
A gift used for the common good becomes a public trust.
stories.summary: When the king's dream baffled his courtiers, Yusuf — still in prison — interpreted it: seven years of plenty would be followed by seven years of famine, and advised storing grain during the good years. The king, impressed, summoned him and placed him in charge of the storehouses.
stories.title: Yusuf — Interpreting Dreams

stories.context: During the famine, Yusuf's brothers came to Egypt for grain. He tested them, revealed himself, and forgave them completely.
lessons: Forgiveness after power is the highest form of strength.
A wrong can be repaired without humiliating the wrongdoer.
Family bonds can survive even betrayal.
stories.summary: The brothers came seeking grain and did not recognise the minister before them. Yusuf tested them, then revealed himself: 'I am Yusuf, and this is my brother.' He forgave them without reproach, brought his parents to Egypt, and thanked Allah for the dream's fulfilment.
stories.title: Yusuf — Reunion and Forgiveness

stories.context: Ayyub lost his wealth, his children and his health, yet remained patient and turned to Allah in prayer.
lessons: Patience is not the absence of pain but endurance through it.
Calling on Allah in affliction is itself worship.
Relief, when it comes, can exceed what was lost.
stories.summary: Ayyub endured prolonged affliction and called upon Allah, saying that hardship had touched him and Allah is the Most Merciful. Allah answered him, removed his affliction, and restored his family and wealth as a mercy and a reminder for worshippers.
stories.title: Ayyub — Patience in Affliction

stories.context: Shuaib was sent to Midian, whose people cheated in trade and blocked the roads. He called them to fair measure and honest dealing.
lessons: Honesty in business is part of faith, not separate from it.
Cheating customers is corruption, however small the measure.
A community's economy reflects its morals.
stories.summary: Shuaib told his people to give full measure and weight, not to defraud others, and not to spread corruption. They mocked him and threatened him, but he persisted. A mighty blast seized the rejecters, and Shuaib and the believers were saved.
stories.title: Shuaib — Honest Measure

stories.context: Musa, tending flocks in Midian, saw a fire on the mountain and found himself addressed by Allah from a blessed valley.
lessons: A call can come in the middle of ordinary work.
Remove distractions — even sandals — before sacred words.
Fear can turn into strength when Allah says, 'Do not fear.'
stories.summary: Musa saw a fire and went to it hoping for a brand or guidance. From the fire came the voice: 'I am Allah.' His staff became a serpent and his hand shone white. He asked for his brother Harun as a helper, and Allah granted it, sending them both to Pharaoh.
stories.title: Musa — The Burning Bush

stories.context: Musa and Harun confronted Pharaoh, who claimed divinity and enslaved the Israelites. The contest with Pharaoh's magicians ended with the magicians believing.
lessons: Truth does not need Pharaoh's permission to be spoken.
Even hired opponents can recognise truth when they see it.
Tyranny's first response to truth is mockery, then force.
stories.summary: Musa showed Pharaoh the signs — the staff that became a serpent and the shining hand — but Pharaoh called it magic and summoned his magicians. Their ropes and staffs seemed to move, but Musa's staff swallowed them. The magicians fell down believing, though Pharaoh threatened them with punishment.
stories.title: Musa — Before Pharaoh

stories.context: Pharaoh's army pursued the Israelites to the sea. Allah parted the waters, the Israelites crossed, and Pharaoh's host drowned.
lessons: When every road is closed, the sea itself can open.
A pursuer's power ends where Allah's command begins.
Deliverance and destruction can happen in the same waters.
stories.summary: By Allah's command, Musa led his people out by night. At the sea, with Pharaoh's army behind them, the people despaired, but Musa struck the sea and it parted into dry paths. The Israelites crossed safely; Pharaoh and his army, following in, were drowned.
stories.title: Musa — The Exodus and the Sea

stories.context: While Musa was on the mountain receiving the tablets, some of his people made a golden calf and worshipped it.
lessons: A community can relapse the moment its leader is absent.
Gold can become an idol when patience runs out.
A leader's anger must be followed by intercession, not abandonment.
stories.summary: Musa went to the mountain for forty nights. In his absence, Samiri made a calf from the people's gold, and many worshipped it. Musa returned in anger, seized Harun, and then prayed for forgiveness for himself and his brother. The calf was burned and scattered in the sea.
stories.title: Musa — The Golden Calf

stories.context: Harun, Musa's brother, shared the mission: he spoke for Musa, stayed with the people, and bore their pressure with patience.
lessons: A helper's role is itself a prophetic honour.
Speaking for truth takes a different courage than leading.
Restraint under pressure can be wiser than force.
stories.summary: Musa asked Allah to make Harun his minister, to strengthen him and share his task. Harun stood beside Musa before Pharaoh and stayed with the people when Musa went to the mountain, counselling patience when they turned to the calf.
stories.title: Harun — The Brother and Helper

stories.context: Dawud, a shepherd who became king, was given the Zabur and a voice so beautiful that mountains and birds joined his praise.
lessons: Leadership and devotion belong together.
Justice must be judged by evidence, even against oneself.
A beautiful voice is a trust to be used in praise, not pride.
stories.summary: Dawud was given wisdom, kingship and the Zabur. The Quran recalls his repentance after judging a dispute between two litigants, and how Allah strengthened his kingdom. His praise was joined, in the Quran's imagery, by mountains and birds.
stories.title: Dawud — The Psalmist King

stories.context: Sulayman understood the speech of birds and, passing through a valley of ants, smiled at an ant's warning to its colony.
lessons: Power is complete only when it listens to the smallest voices.
A smile at a small creature shows a great heart.
Gratitude for a gift is part of the gift itself.
stories.summary: Sulayman, heir to Dawud, was taught the speech of birds and marched with armies of jinn, humans and birds. In a valley of ants, he heard an ant warn its fellows to enter their dwellings lest Sulayman's hosts crush them unknowingly — and he smiled and thanked Allah for His favour.
stories.title: Sulayman — Wisdom and the Ant Valley

stories.context: Sulayman received word of a queen in Sheba who worshipped the sun. He invited her to Allah, and she came and submitted.
lessons: Diplomacy can precede force, and often replaces it.
A wise ruler tests reports before acting on them.
Submission to truth is not defeat but dignity.
stories.summary: The hoopoe brought Sulayman news of a queen ruling Sheba, whose people worshipped the sun. Sulayman sent her a letter inviting submission. She came, recognised the signs, and declared her submission to Allah with Sulayman, after mistaking his glass palace floor for water.
stories.title: Sulayman — The Queen of Sheba

stories.context: Ilyas called his people, who worshipped Baal, back to Allah, but they rejected him.
lessons: Calling people away from inherited idols is lonely work.
A prophet's success is not measured by the crowd's response.
Patience with a rejecting people is itself faithfulness.
stories.summary: Ilyas told his people to fear Allah and abandon Baal, the idol they worshipped, but they called him a liar. The Quran records that he was left with a good name among later generations, while those who rejected the message faced its consequence.
stories.title: Ilyas — The Call to His People

stories.context: Al-Yasa is named in the Quran among the righteous prophets, a successor in the line of guidance.
lessons: Continuing a predecessor's work is itself a prophetic task.
The Quran honours some prophets with a name and no long story.
Steadfastness in an unrecorded life is still recorded with Allah.
stories.summary: Al-Yasa is mentioned in the Quran among the excellent and righteous, alongside Ismail and Dhul-Kifl. No extended narrative about him is given in the Quran; classical scholars place him as a successor carrying on the guidance of Ilyas.
stories.title: Al-Yasa — The Successor

stories.context: Yunus left his people in anger before their punishment came, was swallowed by a great fish, and called out from the darkness.
lessons: Leaving a task in anger is itself a mistake to repent.
Darkness — of sea, night and belly — cannot hide a sincere call.
A whole city's repentance can turn away punishment.
stories.summary: Yunus departed from his people before permission came and boarded a laden ship. Cast into the sea, he was swallowed by a great fish and called out from the darkness, glorifying Allah and confessing his wrong. He was cast onto the shore, and his people — who had believed — were granted respite.
stories.title: Yunus — The Man of the Whale

stories.context: Dhul-Kifl is named in the Quran among the patient and righteous, though no story about him is narrated there.
lessons: Patience is a rank, not just a feeling.
Some of the righteous are known to Allah by a name alone.
Keeping a trust faithfully is a form of prophecy's work.
stories.summary: Dhul-Kifl is mentioned in the Quran among the patient and the righteous, together with Ismail and Idris. The Quran gives no further narrative about him; classical scholars offer various identifications, which are not settled by the Quranic text itself.
stories.title: Dhul-Kifl — The Patient One

stories.context: Zakariya, old and childless, prayed privately for an heir, and was given Yahya.
lessons: Private prayer is not less powerful than public prayer.
Old age does not close the door of Allah's gift.
An answered prayer should be met with more devotion, not less.
stories.summary: Zakariya called upon Allah in secret, asking for an heir despite his old age and his wife's barrenness. Angels gave him glad tidings of Yahya, a name never given before. He asked for a sign and was told he would not speak to people for three nights, though sound.
stories.title: Zakariya — A Prayer Answered

stories.context: Yahya, son of Zakariya, was given wisdom as a youth, and is described as chaste, dutiful to his parents, and not arrogant.
lessons: Wisdom can come early to a pure heart.
Dutifulness to parents is part of prophethood's character.
Chastity and humility are strengths, not softness.
stories.summary: The Quran says Yahya was given wisdom while still a boy, and describes him as compassionate, pure, dutiful to his parents, and neither arrogant nor rebellious. Peace is pronounced upon him on the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.
stories.title: Yahya — The Chaste Prophet

stories.context: Maryam, alone and in labour, was told not to grieve; a stream and ripe dates were provided for her, and her child spoke from the cradle.
lessons: Provision can come to the one who is most alone.
A mother's dignity is defended by Allah Himself.
A miracle does not remove the hardship around it.
stories.summary: Maryam withdrew to a distant place and gave birth beneath a palm tree. She was told to shake the trunk for ripe dates and to drink from a stream. When her people questioned her, the infant Isa spoke from the cradle, declaring himself a servant of Allah, a prophet given the Book.
stories.title: Isa — The Birth

stories.context: Isa was given the Gospel, healed the blind and the leper, and raised the dead by Allah's permission, calling his people to worship Allah alone.
lessons: Miracles point to Allah; they are not ends in themselves.
A prophet's message is worship of Allah alone.
Gratitude for a gift is shown by using it for others.
stories.summary: The Quran describes Isa as the Messiah, a word from Allah, strengthened with the Holy Spirit. He fashioned a bird from clay and breathed life into it by Allah's permission, healed the blind and the leper, and raised the dead — all as signs, while calling his people to worship Allah, his Lord and theirs.
stories.title: Isa — Miracles and Message

stories.context: In the cave of Hira, Muhammad received the first words of revelation: a command to read in the name of his Lord who created.
lessons: The first command of revelation is to read and learn.
A mission can begin in solitude, far from crowds.
Trembling at a great encounter is human; returning to it is faith.
stories.summary: The Quran's first revealed words commanded reading in the name of the Lord who created humanity from a clinging clot, who taught by the pen and taught humanity what it did not know. Classical accounts describe this moment in the cave of Hira, where the Prophet received the revelation and returned home deeply moved.
stories.title: Muhammad — The First Revelation
